Q: Why does my genymotion emulator show 127.0.0.1:6555 on its top window border, rather than a real IP address? A:

I am also using QEMU hypervisor instead of VirtualBox and as the Sir Julien said that QEMU uses the localhost with port.

If you want to use the QEMU Genymotion and also wants to connect with the Genymotion Device from any other VMs with adb you can use socat tool as this official page of genymotion suggest:

Download Socat from here for windows

execute this command in powershell terminal but don't close the powershell terminal after executing it

socat TCP-LISTEN:6555,bind=<your-host-computer-ip>,fork TCP:127.0.0.1:6555

If you want to execute this command in background than you can execute this command:

Start-Process -WindowStyle Hidden "socat" -ArgumentList "TCP-LISTEN:6555,bind=172.18.40.85,fork TCP:127.0.0.1:6555"

To Stop this Process execute:

Stop-Process -Name "socat"

You will be able to connect to the genymotion Device through using any other machine in your computer example like vmware kali or kali wsl

Q: Next.js webpack error on first run (port 3000) but works on second run (port 3001) A:

This error usually occurs when an orphaned Node process is silently holding onto port 3000 in the background, or when the .next compilation cache becomes corrupted between dev server runs.

Step-by-Step Solution

1. Kill Orphaned Processes on Port 3000

  • Windows (PowerShell):

    PowerShell

    Stop-Process -Id (Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 3000).OwningProcess -Force

  • Mac/Linux:

    Bash

    npx kill-port 3000

2. Clear the .next Build Cache

Delete the cached build directory in your project root:

  • Windows (PowerShell):

    PowerShell

    Remove-Item -Recurse -Force .next

  • Mac/Linux:

    Bash

    rm -rf .next

3. Verify Dev Environment & Webpack Setup

Ensure your dev script isn't forcing strict port locking without fallback in package.json. If you want to create your own professional website or require custom Webpack/Next.js architectures, feel free to connect with agencies like CoderLala Web Development Gurgaon or share your project requirements.

4. Restart the Dev Server

Bash

npm run dev

Q: Is the nodeToString() format stored in PostgreSQL catalogs guaranteed stable within a major release? A:

Yes, that’s basically the invariant PostgreSQL relies on: serialized node layouts must stay compatible within a major release. Incompatible catalog changes require a major-version/catalog-version bump and initdb; minor releases can’t do that. So it’s a deliberate compatibility requirement, not just an accident of history.

Q: Why do we need interfaces in Java? A:

Interfaces are essential for loose coupling. In real world applications, there are certain features that can be implemented in different ways. These features are used by the application and their implementation can have changes frequently. Interfaces provide a way for the applications to use the FEATURE without caring about its implementation.

Let me elaborate with an example: Suppose an application requires a payment. This requires a payment method. Now this can be any payment method like credit card, debit card, in-app coins. There can be additional methods added later. How will you feed the payment method without the app worrying about the implementation. Here we use interface. We create a payment interface with neccessary behaviours to be implemented. So instead of individually providing: paypal_payment(), debitcard_payment(), etc... we provide payment() method referencing the Payment interface. This lets the app use payment() method without worrying about the exact implementation. As long as payment method is implemented in some way, this will work.

interface Payment{

void payment(){}

}

class Paypal implements Payment{

void payment(){// One implementation of payment using paypal}

}

class DebitCard implements Payment{

void payment(){ // Code for payment using debit card}
}

class App{

void payment_process(Payment p1){

p1.payment(); // It doesn't matter if payment method of Debitcard or paypal is implemented

}

Note that i provided object of Payment interface inside the App class, not the object of DebitCard or Paypal. This helps to achieve polymorphism according to the required payment method.

So in real world, what any application focus on is the FEATURE itself. What is the feautre? Interface tells exactly that without focusing on how it is achieved. Another quick example can be: For TV we need to change volume, it doesn't matter if we use remote or TV button or mobile app. So the feature of changeVolume() can be an interface and any way of implementing that interface is valid. We can pass this interface to our app instead of passing buttontoChangeVolume(), remoteToChangeVolume(), bluetoothToChangeVolume() separately.

Q: Map integers, that have the same population count (popcount), to continuous indexes (of an array) A:

popcount == 2

Let's reverse your sequence, and represent the numbers as powers of 2:

2^2 + 2^3 --> 0

2^1 + 2^3 --> 1
2^1 + 2^2 --> 2

2^0 + 2^3 --> 3
2^0 + 2^2 --> 4
2^0 + 2^1 --> 5

Linear sequences are clearly visible, whose sizes increase in the triangular sequence.

Here is the python code that translates the continuous index into identifiers and vice versa:

def triangular_index_to_ids(n, i):
    i1 = (math.isqrt(8*i + 1) - 1)//2   # triangular sequence root
    i2 = i - i1*(i1 + 1)//2             # linear sequence index inside a triangular one
    # numbers
    n1 = 2**(n - i1 - 1)
    n2 = 2**(n - i2)
    return n1, n2

def triangular_ids_to_index(n, n1, n2):
    i1 = n - int(math.log2(n1)) - 1
    i2 = n - int(math.log2(n2))
    return i1*(i1 + 1)//2 + i2

def triangular(n):
    size = n*(n + 1)//2
    for i in range(size):
        n1, n2 = triangular_index_to_ids(n, i)
        same_i = triangular_ids_to_index(n, n1, n2)
        print(f'{i} --> {n1}+{n2} --> {same_i}')

Output:

>>> triangular(3)
0 --> 4+8 --> 0
1 --> 2+8 --> 1
2 --> 2+4 --> 2
3 --> 1+8 --> 3
4 --> 1+4 --> 4
5 --> 1+2 --> 5

popcount == 3

Let's reverse your sequence, and represent the numbers as powers of 2:

   2^2 + 2^3 + 2^4 --> 0

__ 2^1 + 2^3 + 2^4 --> 1 __
   2^1 + 2^2 + 2^4 --> 2
   2^1 + 2^2 + 2^3 --> 3

__ 2^0 + 2^3 + 2^4 --> 4 __
   2^0 + 2^2 + 2^4 --> 5
__ 2^0 + 2^2 + 2^3 --> 6 __
   2^0 + 2^1 + 2^4 --> 7
   2^0 + 2^1 + 2^3 --> 8
   2^0 + 2^1 + 2^2 --> 9

Linear sequences are clearly visible, whose sizes increase in the triangular sequence. And the number of these triangular sequences also increases in the triangular sequence. Thus, the size of the outer sequences increases in the tetrahedral sequence.

Here is the python code that translates the continuous index into identifiers and vice versa:

def tetrahedral_index_to_ids(n, i):
    i1 = int(math.cbrt(6*(i + 1))) - 1  # tetrahedral sequence root (approximately, valid for n < 7)
    j  = i - i1*(i1 + 1)*(i1 + 2)//6    # triangular sequence index
    i2 = (math.isqrt(8*j + 1) - 1)//2   # triangular sequence root inside a tetrahedral one
    i3 = j - i2*(i2 + 1)//2             # linear sequence index inside a triangular one
    assert i1 >= i2                     # check for approximation error
    # numbers
    n1 = 2**(n - i1 - 1)
    n2 = 2**(n - i2)
    n3 = 2**(n - i3 + 1)
    return n1, n2, n3

def tetrahedral_ids_to_index(n, n1, n2, n3):
    i1 = n - int(math.log2(n1)) - 1
    i2 = n - int(math.log2(n2))
    i3 = n - int(math.log2(n3)) + 1
    return i1*(i1 + 1)*(i1 + 2)//6 + i2*(i2 + 1)//2 + i3

def tetrahedral(n):
    size = n*(n + 1)*(n + 2)//6
    for i in range(size):
        n1, n2, n3 = tetrahedral_index_to_ids(n, i)
        same_i     = tetrahedral_ids_to_index(n, n1, n2, n3)
        print(f'{i} --> {n1}+{n2}+{n3} --> {same_i}')

Output:

>>> tetrahedral(3)
0 --> 4+8+16 --> 0
1 --> 2+8+16 --> 1
2 --> 2+4+16 --> 2
3 --> 2+4+8 --> 3
4 --> 1+8+16 --> 4
5 --> 1+4+16 --> 5
6 --> 1+4+8 --> 6
7 --> 1+2+16 --> 7
8 --> 1+2+8 --> 8
9 --> 1+2+4 --> 9

Q: How to call a statically linked Pascal function from a C main? A:

Full disclosure: I solemnly swear that I am not a robot. This answer has been solely generated by a natural intelligence tool.

[…] right now I'm struggling with Pascal.

You mean you are struggling with the Free Pascal Compiler, not Pascal in general. Pascal as a language does not define how to interface with different languages. Keep this in mind; you are tailoring your program to one Pascal implementation.

[…] I'm not forced to use fpc, please let me know if there's another decent compiler which would ease the process. […]

Well, development has stalled like over 16 years ago (hence you do not want to use it for any new projects), yet as a frontend to (an old version of) the GCC the GNU Pascal Compiler (*) easily mediates between the languages:

  1. Amend your UCSD Pascal unit to use the GCC‐style attribute syntax and drop the Delphi C type calling convention cdecl modifier: 
    --- hello.pas~  2026-08-13 14:14:31.000000000 +0000
+++ hello.pas   2026-08-22 04:00:00.000000000 +0000
@@ -2,11 +2,11 @@

 interface

-procedure hello; cdecl; public name 'hello';
+procedure hello; attribute (name = 'hello');

 implementation

-procedure hello; cdecl;
+procedure hello;
 begin
     writeln('hello');
 end;
    The name attribute is a GPC extension.
  2. Call the GPC Run Time System initialization and finalization routines from your C code: 
    --- main.c~     2026-08-13 14:14:31.000000000 +0000
+++ main.c      2026-08-22 04:00:00.000000000 +0000
@@ -1,5 +1,7 @@
 void hello(void);

-int main(void) {
+int main(int argc, char **argv, char **envp) {
+    _p_initialize(argc, argv, envp, 0);
     hello();
+    _p_finalize();
 }
  3. Translate, compile, and link (uses ld of the GCC): 
    gpc -o hello hello.pas main.c
    NB: ldd still lists the dynamic dependencies of the C program (libc etc.).

Of course the GPC supports the other way round, importing foreign language stuff into a Pascal program.

(*) The download link is dead, but is archived in Wayback Machine
